equations.label: base tourist demand
equations.role: update annual tourist count from growth, tourism tax, and an external demand shock
equations.transcription: T(t) = T(t-1) * (1 + g(t) - gamma * tau(t) + delta(t))

equations.label: seasonal tourist split
equations.role: separate peak and off-peak tourist counts through multiplicative seasonal factors
equations.transcription: T_peak(t) = S_peak * T(t); T_off(t) = S_off * T(t); S_peak > 1; S_off < 1

equations.label: policy-adjusted growth and promotion budget
equations.role: reduce baseline growth through a visitor-cap term and increase it through tax-funded promotion
equations.transcription: g(t) = g_base - beta * C_cap(t) + eta * M(t); M(t) = lambda * G(t)

equations.label: tourism revenue
equations.role: convert tourist count to total tourism revenue with fixed average revenue per tourist

equations.label: government tourism-tax revenue
equations.role: apply the tourism tax rate to total tourism revenue

equations.label: tourism operating cost
equations.role: combine fixed operating cost with tourist-proportional variable cost

equations.label: tourism net profit
equations.role: subtract tourism operating cost from tourism revenue

equations.label: min-max normalization
equations.role: normalize an environmental variable to the unit interval

equations.label: entropy
equations.role: measure dispersion of a normalized environmental variable

equations.label: entropy weight
equations.role: convert each variable entropy into a relative environmental weight

equations.label: environmental index
equations.role: aggregate weighted normalized environmental factors and min-max normalize the aggregate

equations.label: government environmental intervention
equations.role: add a spending-mediated intervention increment to the environmental state

equations.label: environmental recovery
equations.role: combine the intervened environmental state, natural recovery, and tourist pressure
equations.transcription: E(t+1) = E_sub(t) + r * (1 - E_sub(t)) - h * (T(t) / T_max)

equations.label: resident satisfaction
equations.role: combine distance from an optimal tourist count, environmental quality, and tourism tax
equations.transcription: Q(t) = omega_1 * (1 - abs(T(t) - T_opt) / T_opt) + omega_2 * E(t) - omega_3 * tau(t)

equations.label: Bellman recursion
equations.role: maximize current profit, environmental quality, resident satisfaction, and discounted continuation value
equations.transcription: V(t) = max_{tau(t), M(t)} {P(t) + omega_4 * E(t) + omega_5 * Q(t) + gamma * V(t+1)}

equations.label: tourist carrying-capacity constraint
equations.role: bound tourist count by Juneau infrastructure carrying capacity

equations.label: environmental floor constraint
equations.role: retain a minimum acceptable environmental index

equations.label: resident-satisfaction floor constraint
equations.role: retain a minimum resident satisfaction index

equations.label: government budget constraint
equations.role: keep government expenditure within tax revenue

equations.label: Miami cultural index
equations.role: aggregate normalized cultural indicators with entropy-derived weights

equations.label: Miami tourist demand
equations.role: extend Juneau demand with a cultural-attractiveness term
equations.transcription: T(t) = T(t-1) * (1 + g(t) - gamma * tau(t) + delta(t) + eta * C(t))

equations.label: Miami resident satisfaction
equations.role: extend satisfaction with cultural value and a fourth tax coefficient
equations.transcription: Q(t) = omega_1 * (1 - abs(T(t) - T_opt) / T_opt) + omega_2 * E(t) + omega_3 * C(t) - omega_4 * tau(t)

fact_checks.observation: The Summary names four linked model components, a five-year Juneau policy path, one-factor sensitivity, Miami transfer, and a tax recommendation before keywords.
The visually recovered Contents accounts for every substantive section, the memo, and the AI-use report.
The Introduction binds 1.6 million 2023 cruise passengers to Mendenhall retreat, traffic, public services, and resident concerns; Figure 1 carries both place and pressure evidence.
Research objectives and Our Work hand demand, economy, environment, satisfaction, dynamic programming, sensitivity, and transfer into Figure 2.
Eight assumptions visibly precede Table 1; they simplify causation, revenue, recovery, seasonality, shocks, and policy finance.
Table 2 contains 2019-2023 Juneau tourist, revenue, attitude, temperature, snowfall, ocean-temperature, and pH values, including pandemic zeros.
The paper explicitly keeps pandemic outliers to infer environmental and social development without tourists, then shows a linear revenue fit and three sustainability objectives.
Equations (1)-(2) define annual demand, tax elasticity, random shock, and stable peak/off-peak multipliers; Figure 5 shows the five-year series.
The recovered page defines g_base, beta, eta, lambda, C_cap, M, R, G, and C through Equations (3)-(6).
Equation (7) closes the economic branch, Figure 6 plots revenue, and Equation (8) opens environmental min-max normalization.
Equations (9)-(12) move from entropy and weights through a normalized aggregate and an intervention-adjusted environmental state; Figure 7 visualizes the computation.
Equations (13)-(14) define recovery, tourist harm, optimal-tourist distance, environmental value, and tax disutility; Figure 8 maps the state-policy framework.
Equation (15) states the Bellman objective and Equations (16)-(19) state tourist, environmental, satisfaction, and budget constraints.
The paper names T, E, Q states and tau, M decisions, restates three transitions, and describes backward recursion plus forward traceback around Figure 9.
Table 3 and Figure 10 report five years of tourists, tax, government revenue, environmental index, and resident satisfaction.
Figure 11 allocates government expenditures among environment, infrastructure, subsidies, and advertising and accompanies a policy interpretation.
Figures 12-13 show four policy outputs under separate sweeps of average environmental index and resident satisfaction.
The recovered text and Figure 14 complete resident-satisfaction interpretation and sweep average tourist count.
Figure 15 and prose contrast Miami and Juneau and introduce demographic, migration, revenue, event, cultural, and financial inputs without a frozen dataset.
fact_checks.target: Miami data and cultural index setup

fact_checks.observation: Equation (20), Figure 16, and Table 4 connect entropy-weighted culture to destination-specific model adjustments.
Table 5 reports five Miami years, and Equations (21)-(22) add culture to tourist demand and resident satisfaction.
Dynamic caps, tax differentiation, promotion, five strengths, and the start of four weaknesses follow the Miami transfer.
The paper completes data, simplification, stakeholder, and computational limitations, then lists only five references.
The council memo repeats the 4.2 percent initial tax, 3.2-5.0 percent path, four spending areas, five-year outputs, adaptive policy, monitoring, and feedback recommendations.
The AI-use report discloses Ernie 4.0 assistance for Juneau factor framing, Juneau-Miami comparison, and dynamic-programming formulation; this page is excluded from positive author-language evidence.

g7_warnings.warning: Watermarks, QR blocks, Chinese publisher/footer material, Contents, References, and the AI-use report are not positive author-language evidence.
Page 25 discloses Ernie 4.0 outputs; the disclosure itself cannot support human-style language patterns.
Generic Juneau key-factor framing overlaps the first disclosed AI query and must not be promoted as confirmed human-authored phrasing.
State, decision, transition, reward, recursion, and backward-programming prose overlaps the third disclosed AI query and is retained as model evidence, not confirmed human-style evidence.
Generic Juneau-Miami comparison prose overlaps the second disclosed AI query and is retained with uncertain authorship.
NOAA, CBJ, Alaska Climate Center, tourism-association, Miami, event, migration, and cultural sources are named incompletely and lack one frozen retrieval ledger.
Only five references are listed although many external data and domain claims appear throughout the paper.
The core calibration table has only five annual observations, two dominated by pandemic disruption.
Keeping 2020-2021 zeros to infer environmental or social development without tourists does not identify tourism's causal effect.
Linear revenue and fixed revenue per tourist suppress visitor mix, price, inflation, season, and capacity effects.
Treating tourism as the only cause of Juneau environmental harm excludes climate, shipping, development, and other drivers.
A constant natural recovery rate is asserted without calibration, seasonality, thresholds, or uncertainty.
S_peak and S_off are assumed stable but no estimation sample, values, fit, or uncertainty is published.
Equation (1) introduces delta(t) without a distribution, scenario path, seed, or propagation into reported results.
The tax elasticity gamma has no source, estimate, unit convention, or uncertainty interval.
Equation (3) subtracts beta times the numerical cap, so a higher allowed cap lowers growth; this is not reconciled with cap stringency or the prose.
M(t)=lambda G(t) fixes promotion as a tax-revenue share but lambda, budget timing, and competing uses are not specified.
M(t) changes meaning among promotion, general government spending, environmental intervention, and multi-category allocation.
Equation (4) uses a fixed per-tourist revenue coefficient without source, year, currency basis, or fit diagnostics.
Equation (5) applies tau to total tourism revenue, but the legal and accounting tax base is not established.
Equation (6) gives fixed and variable costs without values, provenance, depreciation, public-service costs, or uncertainty.
Equation (7) does not reconcile annual revenue, cost timing, government revenue, spending, or monetary units.
Equation (8) does not freeze x_min and x_max, so transfer and future-state comparability are not reproducible.
Equation (9) calls normalized values p_i without showing the probability normalization or the usual sample-size coefficient.
The paper assigns -1 to temperature and ocean temperature before entropy weighting without explaining how negative direction is transformed for logs and probabilities.
Equations (9)-(10) omit complete observation and criterion indexes, zero handling, and the fitted weight values.
Equation (11) aggregates four variables from five years without uncertainty, validation, or stable endpoint treatment.
Equation (12) uses the same M(t) previously defined as tourism promotion and provides no alpha estimate or spending unit conversion.
Equation (13) lacks provenance and units for r, h, and T_max and does not prove E remains in a meaningful range.
Equation (14) is an ad hoc weighted sum with no elicitation, normalization proof, or observed satisfaction fit.
The resident-satisfaction prose names public services and environmental quality, while Equation (14) contains tourist distance, E, and tax only.
Equation (15) directly adds monetary profit to dimensionless E and Q without scaling or stakeholder utility calibration.
gamma denotes tax elasticity in Equation (1) and the discount factor in Equation (15).
C_max, E_min, and Q_min are not numerically frozen or sourced for the reported optimization.
A scalar M(t) cannot reproduce four expenditure shares without additional allocation controls and constraints.
No terminal value, state grid, control grid, interpolation rule, discount value, feasibility handling, or traceback implementation is published.
No code, environment, input bundle, solver trace, checksum, or replay command supports the dynamic-programming results.
Table 3 government revenue cannot be independently reconciled with its tourists, tax rates, Table 2 revenue basis, and the printed linear revenue model.
Resident satisfaction drops from 0.893 to 0.832 in Year 3, so the prose claim of a positive trend is not literally true.
Table 3 and Figure 10 are model-generated outputs, not observed evidence that the policy is effective.
Figure 11 is not backed by a numerical table, annual budget reconciliation, allocation equation, or implementation constraints.
The Juneau results mention cultural investment before culture is defined only in the Miami adaptation.
Figures 12-14 omit baseline values, justified ranges, step sizes, units, sampling design, interactions, and numerical sensitivity metrics.
Direction-only curve readings do not establish robustness, uncertainty intervals, or policy-rank stability.
The Miami transfer names several data classes but supplies no frozen observations, transformations, citations, or calibration ledger.
Figure 16 labels a 2019-2023 cultural and tourist trend without reconciling it to Table 5's generic Years 1-5 or a cited historical series.
Table 5 labels tourist count in thousands, producing 0.804-1.473 million visitors, a scale not reconciled with Miami tourism or the plotted series.
Snow is replaced by ocean and urban-emission factors without printing the revised environmental equation, weights, endpoints, or calibration.
Traffic and culture are mentioned, but only culture appears explicitly in Equation (22), with no fitted weights or observed validation.
Reusing the structure in Miami and reporting outputs is an adaptation demonstration, not external validation or generalizability evidence.
Dynamic caps, differentiated taxes, and targeted promotion are generic recommendations without a destination dataset, optimization result, or quantified distribution effect.
The stated weaknesses omit symbol collisions, unit mixing, missing DP specification, internal-only validation, and AI-provenance risk.
The memo presents model-generated policy outputs as effective recommendations without uncertainty ranges, owners, triggers, monitoring thresholds, or rollback criteria.
Figure 3 is a tourist-revenue regression plot although its caption also claims to show environmental index against tourist count.

page_recoveries.content: Contents: Introduction, Preparation, Models, Sensitivity Analysis, Adaptability, Strengths and Weaknesses, References, Memo, and AI-use report with printed page ownership.

Eight assumptions covering linear revenue, profit maximization and tax, seasons, tax-funded environmental spending, natural recovery, tourism-only environmental harm, bounded growth, and fixed revenue per tourist; Table 1 notation follows.
Policy impact on demand and Equations (3)-(6): visitor-cap and promotion effects on growth, tax-funded M(t), linear tourism revenue, tax revenue, and fixed-plus-variable cost.
Resident-satisfaction sensitivity conclusion and tourist-count sensitivity: subsidies, taxes, advertising, environmental spending, infrastructure, and Figure 14.
